title: My hair was black
hook: Ambapali's song of her aging body: once lovely, now changed; the truth's word never fails (Therigatha, Ambapali)
carry: so it was, so it is

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kisa Gotami's own song put friends first, before grief, kalyanamitta. Your line was good friends. Did you tell a friend plainly what they meant? Today, a woman looks at her own body across the years. Day seven hundred ninety-one.

Black as bees, curled at the tips. That's how Ambapali remembers her hair. The path met her before as the courtesan of Vesali who hosted the Buddha for a meal and gave his community her mango grove. In the Therigatha she is an old nun, and her song walks down her own body, from her hair to her feet, then and now. Every verse ends the same way, and that refrain is today's lesson.
screen: `BLACK AS BEES.` → `A COURTESAN, THEN A NUN.` → `ONE REFRAIN, EVERY VERSE.`

segments.voice: First, then and now. My hair was black, she says, the color of bees, curled at the tips. Now, with age, it's like coarse bark fiber. And then the refrain: not otherwise is the word of the one who speaks the truth. So it was. So it is. Second, the walk. She goes on, part by part. Eyes that shone like jewels, now dim. A voice sweet as a cuckoo's in the forest, now faltering. Teeth once bright, now broken. Each verse holds a then and a now, and each closes with the same line. The repeating is part of the teaching; it settles in, verse by verse. Third, who is speaking. This is the woman who, in the sutta of the Buddha's last journey, wouldn't give up a meal with him for all of Vesali, and then gave his community her grove. A woman who knew what beauty and wealth could buy is the one telling us, steadily, what time did. Fourth, the tone. Some readers hear grief in the song. Others hear something calmer: no complaint, no shame, only accuracy. Near the end she says this body is like an old house with its plaster falling away. And the refrain says the Buddha's word holds: things change. In her mouth that isn't a curse. It's a teaching confirmed, by her own skin.
screen: `BLACK HAIR, NOW LIKE BARK.` · `EYES, VOICE, TEETH: THEN AND NOW.` · `ONCE THE COURTESAN OF VESALI.` · `AN OLD HOUSE, PLASTER FALLING.` · then, large: `SO IT WAS, SO IT IS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at an old photograph. Find one of yourself, on your phone or in a drawer, or call one up from memory. Look at it the way Ambapali looked at herself. Hair then, hair now. Face then, face now. Don't argue with it. Don't praise it. Just name it softly: so it was. Then feel the body you're in right now, breathing, sitting, here. So it is. Let the two sit side by side. The bell holds the time.
Sacca. Truth: the word behind Ambapali's refrain, that the truth-speaker's word holds, as her song walks her own body, then and now. Today's word.

Your line: so it was, so it is. This week the sisters sang of a nun who finally stayed, a flame gone out, washed feet, grieving mothers, a foster mother's thanks, and good friends. Today, catch your reflection once and say the line, with no verdict. Day seven hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Reflection on the body's changes is a traditional Buddhist contemplation, and Ambapali's verses are read in Theravada settings as a picture of impermanence seen in one's own body.

fork.setup: you're Ambapali, old now, looking at hair that was once black as bees. what do you say?
options: grieve what's gone, and stop there.
name it plainly, then and now, and say the truth-speaker's word holds.
look away and talk of something else.
fork.reveal: verse by verse she names each change plainly, then and now, and closes each one: not otherwise is the word of the one who speaks the truth.

original.note: Pali sacca: truth. Ambapali's refrain calls the Buddha the one who speaks the truth.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad poem about getting old.
what it means: Ambapali walks through her own body, then and now, and every verse confirms the truth-speaker's word: so it was.
what a scholar hears: the refrain names the Buddha as the speaker of truth; her own body becomes the evidence for his teaching that conditioned things change.
